{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=metric+temporal+logic+formal+verification+epistemic+falsification&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Validating medical digital twins for clinical decision support: beyond predictive accuracy.\", \"abstract\": \"

Objective

To clarify how validation requirements should be specified for medical digital twins used in clinical decision support, particularly when such systems are intended to compare interventions, treatment timings, dosages, or sequential care strategies.

Perspective

Medical digital twins are heterogeneous systems that may combine prediction, simulation, mechanistic modeling, machine learning, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and decision-support functions. Their evaluation should therefore be driven by their intended use rather than by a single definition of what a digital twin is. For digital twins used primarily for visualization, monitoring, or short-term forecasting, predictive accuracy, calibration, discrimination, and robustness may be the central validation targets. However, when digital twins are used to support intervention-oriented clinical decisions, retrospective accuracy under historical clinical practice is insufficient on its own.

Key message

Intervention-oriented digital twins address action-conditioned questions: what is predicted to happen under specified alternative actions, assumptions, time horizons, and clinical contexts. Their validation should therefore extend beyond scalar performance metrics to include uncertainty representation, updating stability, robustness under regime change, action-regime validity, counterfactual consistency, clinically weighted error, and decision-level consequences. This requires drawing on established traditions in forecast verification, causal inference, uncertainty quantification, model verification and validation, decision theory, control theory, and post-deployment monitoring. The level of causal or mechanistic support required should match the clinical claim being made, whether at the genotype, phenotype, physiological, or care-process level.

Conclusion

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=responsibility+artificial+agency+accountability+decision+consequences&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"title\": [\"Accountability Protocol: Decision, Exception, Responsibility\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in organizational and societal decision processes, failures increasingly arise not from technical malfunction but from unresolved boundaries of authority, exception response, and accountability. As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. This paper does not advocate technological restraint, but seeks to clarify the structural conditions under which accountability protocols become necessary.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6238138\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"title\": [\"Determining Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence-Based Security Decision Making\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The chapter discusses the determination of who is responsible when artificial intelligence is used for security decision making within complex organizational environments. {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=artificial+agency+accountability+decision+consequences+moral+responsibility&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Nursing Moral Agency in Technology-Mediated Care: Reclaiming Professional Responsibility in the Fifth Industrial Revolution.\", \"abstract\": \"Nursing practice is increasingly enacted within environments structured by intelligent technologies that filter perception, generate classifications and shape clinical priorities. While nurse scholars have begun to examine moral agency in the context of artificial intelligence, much of the broader ethical discourse on AI in healthcare continues to foreground governance, safety and institutional accountability, leaving the conditions under which nurses exercise professional moral responsibility comparatively under-theorized. This paper argues that technology-mediated care constitutes a moral environment that reshapes how responsibility is distributed, interpreted and enacted in clinical practice. Drawing on nursing ethics and socio-technical thought, it distinguishes between technical delegation and moral delegation, clarifying that while intelligent systems may inform action, they cannot assume moral answerability. Nursing moral agency is reconceptualized as relationally oriented moral perception, interpretive judgement and accountable action that remains fundamentally non-delegable, even under conditions of extensive mediation. Boundary-setting is advanced as a disciplined ethical practice through which nurses delineate the limits of technological authority and sustain professional responsibility. By articulating moral agency as both situated and irreducible, this analysis contributes a conceptual framework for understanding ethical responsibility in the Fifth Industrial Revolution and re-centres the nurse as the accountable moral subject within technology-mediated care.\", \"doi\": \"10.1111/nup.70098\", \"pmid\": \"42462117\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13375117\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1111/nup.70098\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availa…
